headline: ClarityCheck exposed 9M+ photos of people's faces, emails, and phone numbers
summary: The reverse image search tool ClarityCheck left 450 GB of images, including faces of adults, teens, and children, in an unsecured Amazon S3 bucket for months, alongside email addresses and phone numbers.
details: The people-search tool ClarityCheck publicly exposed over 9 million image files, totaling roughly 450 GB, which included photographs of people's faces. This data, stored in an unsecured Amazon S3 bucket, also contained images of adults, teenagers, and children. A separate misconfiguration additionally exposed people's email addresses and phone numbers.

Independent security researcher Jeremiah Fowler discovered the vulnerability, noting that the image files were in folders named 'faces' and 'profiles'. These files were accessible to anyone online through a URL found in the company's publicly available website code.

ClarityCheck is one of several 'people-finder' tools that claim to identify individuals by searching the web, public records, and other databases. Despite its website stating that reverse image searches are 'private and secure,' the exposure contradicted this claim.

Although ClarityCheck secured the massive image database after WIRED contacted the company in July, Fowler warns that it was seemingly exposed for months. His initial attempts to alert the company to the problem were reportedly unsuccessful.

ClarityCheck disputed the characterization of the data as 'publicly exposed,' stating that access required knowledge of a specific, unindexed URL not discoverable through ordinary use. However, the security industry and US federal government consider data exposed if it's accessible without authentication to unintended parties.

The company also stated that the data included duplicate, cropped, and resized copies, not 9 million unique images, along with non-image data. ClarityCheck has since improved its security reporting procedures to facilitate future researcher contact.

headline_marked: [[Playable Doom ported to DSLR camera]] with 3-inch TFT LCD, even plays sound
headline: Playable Doom ported to DSLR camera with 3-inch TFT LCD, even plays sound
summary: A programmer successfully ported the classic shooter Doom to a Canon EOS 550D DSLR, utilizing its 3-inch TFT LCD display and built-in mono speaker for full gameplay.
details: Developer lauris-nl achieved a new feat in the 'Doom on weird hardware' challenge by porting the game to a Canon EOS 550D digital SLR camera. This was made possible using the open-source Magic Lantern firmware, which unlocks additional camera features.

The Canon EOS 550D, also known as the Rebel T2i, was launched in 2010 and features an 18-megapixel APS-C sensor, a DIGIC 4 image processor, and a 3-inch TFT LCD display. The camera's physical buttons are remapped for in-game controls, with the D-pad for movement and the SET button for firing.
The port runs smoothly on the camera, including in-game sounds via its rear mono speaker. The Menu button opens the game's menu, and the DISP. button navigates back.

It's crucial to note that this specific port only works on the Canon EOS 550D with firmware version 1.0.9. Installing it on other camera models or firmware versions is not recommended and carries the risk of bricking the device.

Installation involves copying the module to an SD card with a compatible Magic Lantern 550D.109 build, creating a DOOM folder, and placing Doom-compatible WAD files inside. After restarting the camera, Doom can be launched from the Magic Lantern Games menu.

This project offers a unique way to play the classic game, though it's advised to keep game files on a separate SD card from your photos. Another developer has also created a Doom port for the 2007 Canon PowerShot SD1000 / IXUS 70 point-and-shoot camera.
